title: Batch admission & KV compaction with fallback continuum for OOM resilience
creator: Aisha Patel
body:
Background: In the last two production incidents we saw OOMs correlated with concurrent long-context chat sessions plus bulk streaming batches. Continuous batching improves throughput but allows more KV retention pressure: active KV + new prefixes push aggregate memory past GPU limits. Current mitigations (simple LRU eviction + model fallback) are reactive and cause high tail latency or user-visible failures.

Goal: Implement a multi-stage, policy-driven memory containment system that prevents OOMs proactively while degrading behavior in predictable steps (the fallback continuum). The system must be conservative by default, observable, and reversible with minimal API surface changes. Key outcomes: near-zero uncaught OOMs, bounded latency regressions during high pressure, and clear telemetry to drive automatic vs. manual rollouts.

Design summary: Three coordinated subsystems: 1) Batch Admission Controller (BAC), 2) KV Compaction Engine (KCE), and 3) Fallback Continuum Router (FCR).

1) Batch Admission Controller (BAC):
- Purpose: keep instantaneous GPU memory reserved for in-flight batches below safe thresholds by controlling batch admission.
- Behavior: per-GPU admission window tracks estimated post-batch memory delta (model state + reserved KV + expected token allocation). Admission decisions: accept, accept-with-slow-path (streaming decode, lower parallelism), or reject (return transient 429 with retry guidance).
- Algorithm: maintain EWMA of per-request KV delta sizes and per-token decode memory; combine with global safety margin. Admission thresholds configurable per-customer tier and per-model-profile.

2) KV Compaction Engine (KCE):
- Purpose: reduce resident KV footprint proactively without discarding high-value keys.
- Techniques implemented: segment compaction (merge adjacent KV entries that share prefix context), micro-quantization of cold KV tensors (8->4-bit packing on the fly for cold candidates), and priority-driven soft-eviction (score = recency * request-weight + semantic-importance).
- Behavior: KCE runs continuously with three lanes: hot (no compaction), warm (light packing), cold (full compaction + eviction). Transition policy based on hit-rate and time-since-last-use. Compaction is cooperative and pausable to avoid compute spikes.

3) Fallback Continuum Router (FCR):
- Purpose: deterministic, staged degradation path when memory pressure persists after BAC and KCE steps.
- Stages (in ascending severity):
  a) Thin decode: reduce per-request parallel decode threads and enable sub-token streaming to reduce peak temporary buffers.
  b) Quantized model variant: transparently route to a lower-memory quantized variant (interface-compatible); log divergence metrics.
  c) Spill-to-dedicated-workers: route excess requests to warm CPU-backed spill workers that run partial decoding and return compact deltas.
  d) Controlled reject + retry: final stage returns informative 429 with backoff hints and a token allowing priority admission when capacity frees.
- Routing decisions are deterministic, per-request, and carry metadata to reconstruct end-to-end traces for debugging.

Retries & Idempotency: All client-visible rejections include an idempotency token and estimated retry-after. Internal retry policy uses exponential backoff with randomized jitter and a capped retry budget to avoid amplification.

Observability & Telemetry: New metrics and logs required: oom_incidents (should trend to 0), batch_admit_rejections, admitted_with_slowpath_rate, kv_compaction_bytes_reclaimed, kv_compaction_latency, fallback_stage_rates (per-stage counters), tail_latency_99_9, fallback_quality_delta (BLEU/ROUGE-like proxies for generative divergence), and cost_delta_by_fallback. Dashboards: memory-resilience overview and per-GPU heatmaps. Alerts: sustained batch_admit_rejections > threshold or kv_compaction_latency spikes.

API/Compatibility: No changes to public API. FCR routes are transparent to SDK callers; we will version-models and expose optional header X-Redwood-Fallback-Stage in internal debug mode.

Testing & Rollout:
- Unit tests for admission logic, compaction correctness, and routing rules.
- Staging load tests replicating multi-tenant long-context traces and spike scenarios.
- Chaos tests: inject KV retention noise and simulate slow compaction to validate progressive stages.
- Canary rollout: start with 2% production traffic, ramp by 2x/day while tracking fallback rates and quality proxies.

Operational runbook (summary):
- If fallback_stage_rates increase > 0.5% and user complaints rise, immediately reduce BAC aggressiveness (increase headroom) and enable more aggressive KCE compaction lanes.
- If quality_delta > SLA threshold for a customer, pin that customer's traffic off FCR and open incident.

Privacy & Security: Compaction and KV routing operate on encrypted tensors in memory; KCE will not store compacted data on disk. No new PII paths introduced.

Expected trade-offs: KCE CPU overhead and additional kernels for compaction; slight accuracy delta when routing to quantized variants; more complex scheduling logic. We accept these in exchange for predictable avoidance of catastrophic OOMs and improved uptime.
acceptance_criteria: No uncaught OOMs in controlled staging under 1.5x peak load
BAC rejects/slowpath <= configured SLO for P99 latency impact during 3rd party load tests
KCE reclaims >= 30% of cold-KV memory within 60s for synthetic workloads
Fallback routing produces <1% high-severity quality regressions vs baseline on eval set
Canary ramp to 100% with automated rollback if fallback_stage_rates exceed 3% for more than 1 hour
notes: Tradeoffs: aggressive compaction risks increasing decode CPU; compaction lanes must be rate-limited.
We should coordinate with model-onboarding to produce quantized-compatible variants for all supported models before wide rollout.
Consider adding a 'memory budget' field to model profiles so BAC can be model-aware rather than only GPU-aware.
